title: Magnonic time crystal with lasing coherence
authors: Jiantao Song, C. K. Wei, Shuhuan Ma, Yiming Pan, Zhijian Chen, Li Yu, Wei Lu, Bimu Yao
abstract: Discrete time crystals (DTC) can respond at an integer multiple of the drive period. Internal order-parameter measurements have advanced studies of this novel non-equilibrium phase of matter; however, turning this order into highly coherent, externally accessible radiation remains challenging: pump-driven nonlinear processes must supply sufficient gain to compensate dissipation while preserving subharmonic stability. Here we realize a room-temperature magnonic time crystal (MTC) with radiation of lasing coherence using a pump-induced magnon mode in yttrium iron garnet. A microwave beat drive produces robust period doubling over a finite parameter range, with spectral signatures of higher-order MTC at stronger driving. The emitted field exhibits linewidth narrowing to 260.0 Hz and a first-order correlation decay time of $995 μs$. Our model links this response to three-magnon confluence, yields a stability region consistent with experiment and predicts a possible transition to chaos. We further map the complex temporal dynamics into frequency-resolved nonlinear features for reservoir computing. These results bridge time-crystalline order and nonlinear information processing through intrinsic magnon-magnon interactions and lasing coherence.
summary: This paper reports the realization of a room-temperature magnonic time crystal exhibiting lasing coherence driven by microwave beating. The research demonstrates that three-magnon interactions provide the necessary gain for this coherent output, confirming period doubling and spectral narrowing. Furthermore, the system's complex temporal dynamics are successfully mapped onto a physical reservoir for nonlinear signal processing.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is realizing highly coherent, externally accessible radiation from Discrete Time Crystals (DTCs) by overcoming gain limitations while maintaining subharmonic stability.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a room-temperature magnonic time crystal exhibiting robust period doubling and lasing coherence, which was also shown to function as a physical reservoir for nonlinear signal processing.
method: The study combines experimental measurements using microwave beat driving on YIG with theoretical modeling based on an effective Hamiltonian and nonlinear scattering models.
model_or_system: The physical system is a magnonic time crystal realized in yttrium iron garnet (YIG) using a pump-induced magnon mode. The dynamics are governed by an effective Hamiltonian incorporating three-magnon interactions ($\hat{H}_{3,reg}$ and $\hat{H}_{3,	imes}$).
key_observables: Linewidth narrowing (to 260.0 Hz), first-order correlation decay time ($\sim 995 \mu$s), and the observation of period doubling (2T, 4T, 8T) in the emitted spectrum.
important_parameters: The system response depends critically on the microwave beat drive parameters, particularly the power of the second drive component ($P_2$), which controls the transition between periodic regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the gain mechanism via three-magnon confluence and uses approximations like linear stability analysis for some model components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spectral transitions from T-periodic to 2T-periodic responses (Fig. 1, 2), the confirmation of period-doubling cascades and chaos (Fig. 3), and the development of laser-like coherence via IQ measurements (Fig. 4).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating the fundamental period-doubling response and coherence (Chunk 1), to mapping out the full nonlinear dynamics, including period-doubling cascades and chaos (Chunk 2), and finally applying the system's coherent output to function as a physical reservoir for nonlinear computation (Chunk 3).
why_interesting: This work bridges concepts from non-equilibrium quantum dynamics (time crystals) with practical quantum optics (lasing coherence) and information theory (reservoir computing) using magnonics, making it highly relevant to open quantum systems research.

Spintronics.note: The study directly involves magnons (spin waves) in a magnetic material (YIG) exhibiting coherent emission and lasing, which falls squarely into the quantum-optics/spintronics interface, particularly concerning magnon-photon coupling.
